stages.title: LEARNING ROAD MAP: ASK THE LOCATION QUESTION IN THE RIGHT ORDER
stages.terms: Learning road map: ask the location question in the right order: Industrial geography is not a plant-list chapter.
stages.mechanism: Trap: A named factory is evidence only when it proves a mechanism.
stages.consequence: Industrial geography is not a plant-list chapter.
stages.trap: Industrial geography is not a plant-list chapter.
stages.answer: !Road map from definitions to location, regions and answers

stages.title: TERMINOLOGY FIREWALL: INDUSTRY, MANUFACTURING, FACTORY AND INDUSTRIAL REGION
stages.terms: Industry is the broad set of activities and organisations that transform inputs into useful goods.
stages.mechanism: A corridor links nodes through freight, utilities and urban systems.
stages.consequence: Industry is the broad set of activities and organisations that transform inputs into useful goods.
stages.trap: Visual first: activity, establishment and region are different units and should not be mixed.

stages.title: MAIN LOCATION FACTORS: BUILD A RANKED FACTOR SYSTEM
stages.terms: Main location factors: build a ranked factor system: Ask which input is bulky, perishable, energy-intensive or skill-intensive.
stages.mechanism: Sugar mills are pulled toward cane because cane is bulky and loses recoverable quality with delay.
stages.consequence: Visual first: location results from interacting material, energy, labour, market, transport, water, capital and technology pulls.
stages.trap: Rank the factors; do not merely list them.
stages.answer: Visual first: location results from interacting material, energy, labour, market, transport, water, capital and technology pulls.

stages.title: WEBER'S LEAST-COST THEORY: LEARN IT IN SIX STEPS
stages.terms: Weber's least-cost theory: learn it in six steps: The first task is to find the site with the lowest total cost of moving inputs in and output out.
stages.mechanism: The model gives a disciplined starting mechanism.
stages.consequence: Alfred Weber's 1909 model asks: where can a factory minimise the combined burden of transport cost, labour cost and agglomeration/deglomeration effects?
stages.trap: It is the starting point, not an automatic final answer.
stages.answer: !Weber material index, transport minimum and isodapane

stages.title: TYPES OF INDUSTRIAL ORIENTATION: COMPARE STAGES, NOT LABELS
stages.terms: Types of industrial orientation: compare stages, not labels: Trap: Footloose means flexible among suitable sites, not free from skills, utilities, logistics or regulation.
stages.mechanism: Technology can split the chain: raw-material processing remains near the source while assembly or finishing moves toward markets.
stages.consequence: The term “orientation” does not imprison an industry in one place.
stages.trap: The term “orientation” does not imprison an industry in one place.

stages.title: MAJOR WORLD INDUSTRIAL REGIONS: MAP THE MECHANISM BEHIND EACH BELT
stages.terms: Visual first: the world's major regions represent different combinations of resources, ports, markets, labour and state-supported infrastructure; the map is schematic and not to scale.
stages.mechanism: Use world cases to prove mechanisms, not as decorative examples: Japan refutes resource determinism; Ruhr/Great Lakes show conditional inertia; coastal China shows policy-enabled export agglomeration.
stages.consequence: An industrial region is a historical accumulation.
stages.trap: Visual first: the world's major regions represent different combinations of resources, ports, markets, labour and state-supported infrastructure; the map is schematic and not to scale.

stages.title: AGGLOMERATION, DEGLOMERATION AND INDUSTRIAL INERTIA
stages.terms: Agglomeration means firms cluster because they share
stages.mechanism: Agglomeration means firms cluster because they share
stages.consequence: Agglomeration means firms cluster because they share
stages.trap: The Hugli belt cannot be explained by raw jute alone.

stages.title: ACTORS, INSTITUTIONS AND PLANNED LOCATION: THE STATE CAN SUPPORT, NOT INVENT, EVERY LINKAGE
stages.terms: Actors, institutions and planned location: the state can support, not invent, every linkage: This is an example of deliberate corridor-linked, multimodal and plug-and-play industrial space.
stages.mechanism: The location-theory link is valid: transport, land, labour pools, utilities and market reach are being assembled through policy.
stages.consequence: Basic current anchor retained from the owner
stages.trap: Then state the limit: policy cannot compensate indefinitely for weak market access, skills or ecological capacity.

stages.title: WHAT CHANGED AFTER WEBER - AND WHAT DID NOT
stages.terms: What changes is the content of those burdens.
stages.mechanism: Freight still matters, but time, reliability, qualification by buyers, supplier depth, carbon rules and geopolitical risk may matter more.
stages.consequence: Weber's method remains useful: compare location-dependent burdens.
stages.trap: It is not “location-free”; its cost surface is simply more complex than a mine-market triangle.
stages.answer: !Evolution from classical location theory to modern risk and capability

stages.title: BASIC ANSWER ARCHITECTURE AND EVIDENCE UNITS
stages.terms: Basic answer architecture and evidence units: Claim: Domestic mineral abundance is not necessary for industrialisation.
stages.mechanism: Visual first: high-scoring answers move from a precise boundary to mechanism, evidence, qualification and verdict.
stages.trap: Verdict: Persistence must be demonstrated, not assumed.
